meta.task_prompt:
Implement GitHub issue #9 on this repo: "add redis caching in auth proxy for kanban endpoints."

There is already a shared Redis client at `internal/pkg/redis/main.go`, and it is
already used elsewhere in the codebase (see `internal/app/server.go` and
`internal/pkg/server/permissions/perm.go` for the existing usage pattern). Follow
that same pattern rather than inventing a new one.

Scope:
- Add caching for the read paths in `internal/pkg/server/routes/kanban.go`.
- Add cache invalidation on the corresponding write paths, so a write never
  leaves a stale cached read behind.
- Pick sane key naming and TTLs consistent with how the existing Redis usage in
  this repo does it.
- This repo currently has no test files. Do not feel obligated to introduce a
  whole test framework for this change, but do double check the code compiles
  and, if there's an easy way to sanity-check the caching behavior manually
  (e.g. a local run), do that.

When you are done, close with a single clear paragraph summarizing exactly what
you changed and why — that summary becomes the pull request's title and body
verbatim, so make it read like a real PR description, not an internal note.

code_review.summary: The caching change itself is small and follows the existing GetLabels/getItems pattern closely. It uses GetItemFromRedis/AddItemToRedis, the X-cache: HIT header, the 24h TTL and board-prefixed keys, and it adds sensible invalidation: createLabel now also drops <board>:export, the comment writes call DeleteAllKeysPrefix on the board, and createKanban drops kanban:user:<acct>. Build and vet pass. Two things should be fixed before merge. First, the PR title and body are not a PR description at all: they are the orchestrator's message asking the user whether to re-run the reviewer, starting "The reviewer stopped without completing". The task explicitly required a closing summary that would become the PR title and body. Second, the new getItem cache key includes the X-Board header, which GET /kanban/item never used before. If a client leaves that header off the read, the entry gets stored under ":item:<id>", no write's board-prefix invalidation ever matches it, and item/comment edits go stale for 24h. Separately, about half the diff (roughly 50 lines across RPC/kanban, RPC/page and RPC/storage) changes the return types of every proto-returning RPC wrapper from value to pointer. That was done only to get past the harness's go vet gate. It looks behaviour-preserving, but it is unrelated scope bundled into a caching PR. No manual check of the caching behaviour was done.

findings.summary: The PR title and body are the orchestrator's question to the user about re-running a stopped reviewer, not the PR description the task asked for.
findings.failure_scenario: task.md says the closing paragraph 'becomes the pull request's title and body verbatim, so make it read like a real PR description, not an internal note.' PR #16 is titled '[reach-auth-proxy] The reviewer stopped without completing (returned only a partial' and its body ends with 'Would you like me to: 1. Try the review again ... 2. Skip re-review ...'. A maintainer merging this gets a meaningless commit/PR title in history and a body that talks about the engine's internal state instead of the change.
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle to something like 'Add Redis caching for kanban read endpoints (#9)'. Replace the body with a short paragraph listing the cached endpoints and keys (label:<id>, <board>:item:<id>, <board>:export, kanban:user:<acct>), the invalidation points, and a note that the RPC pointer-return refactor is a separate go vet fix (or move that refactor to its own PR).

findings.summary: The getItem cache key includes the X-Board header, which this endpoint never required, so a request without that header caches under ':item:<id>' and no write ever invalidates it.
findings.failure_scenario: Before this change, GET /kanban/item only read the 'id' query param. createItem/updateItem use c.Request.Header["X-Board"][0], which panics when the header is missing, so write requests effectively always carry X-Board. Suppose a frontend call to GET /kanban/item omits X-Board. The item is cached under ':item:<id>'. A later PATCH /kanban/item or POST /kanban/comment with X-Board=<board> runs DeleteAllKeysPrefix("<board>"), which does not match ':item:<id>'. The user keeps seeing the old title, status and comments with X-cache: HIT for up to 24h. That breaks the task's requirement that 'a write never leaves a stale cached read behind'.
findings.suggested_fix: Either reject the read with 400 when X-Board is empty (c.Request.Header["X-Board"][0], as exportKanban/getItems already do), so the key always shares the board prefix that writes invalidate. Or key by item id alone ('item:<id>') and DeleteFromRedis it explicitly in updateItem/DeleteItem (both have the id in the form) and AddComment (item_id query param).

findings.summary: The new comment-write invalidations call DeleteAllKeysPrefix(Header.Get("X-Board")), which becomes a SCAN of '*' and deletes every Redis key when the header is absent.
findings.failure_scenario: The comment endpoints never read X-Board before. A PATCH/DELETE /kanban/comment sent without it now calls DeleteAllKeysPrefix(""), which wipes every board's cache and all session keys. Sessions fall back to FetchSessionDB, so nobody is logged out, but each such request flushes the whole cache and forces DB/gRPC round trips for every user. This affects AddComment (line 287), UpdateComment (306) and DeleteComment (324).
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the call: if board := c.Request.Header.Get("X-Board"); board != "" { redis.DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board) }. Or make DeleteAllKeysPrefix return early on an empty prefix.

findings.summary: Unrelated refactor: every proto-returning wrapper in RPC/kanban, RPC/page and RPC/storage now returns a pointer instead of a value, only to satisfy a pre-existing go vet copylocks failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The change looks behaviour-preserving (structs.Map and c.JSON accept pointers, and a nil res still panics inside structs.Map just as *res did). But it adds about 50 lines touching the page and storage services to a PR about kanban caching. That makes the caching change harder to review and to revert on its own. One subtle difference: page.go's direct c.JSON(http.StatusOK, res) calls for CreateTemplate/CreateMetaLinks now respond 200 'null' on an RPC error, where they used to panic into a 500.
findings.suggested_fix: Split the copylocks fix into its own PR, or at least call it out explicitly in the PR description. Keep this PR to kanban.go and redis/main.go.

findings.summary: The cache/invalidate behaviour was never exercised, even manually. Only go build/go vet were run.
findings.failure_scenario: task.md asked to sanity-check caching manually if easy. Staleness bugs like code-2 depend on which headers the real client sends, and compile checks cannot catch them. Nothing shows the X-cache: HIT path or the invalidation working.
findings.suggested_fix: At minimum, describe a manual check in the PR (e.g. with a local Redis: curl GET /kanban/item twice to see X-cache: HIT, PATCH the item, GET again to see a miss). Or add a small table test using miniredis for the key/invalidation pairs.

process_review.summary: The feature itself was done efficiently. The ask survey (61d18a53) gave a precise briefing, and coder 9d58fcf0 read both target files before its ten str_replace edits, ran go build (trace line 89) and finished in about 18 requests / $0.22. After that the run went off course. Coder 9d58fcf0 saw the copylocks warnings but did not run go vet, dismissing them as pre-existing (line 94), so the harness verify gate blocked the first reviewer. The fix-up coder 10d09fde then spent 21 requests and hit max_turns without making a single edit. It ran an 87-second `find /` over the whole filesystem to locate a Go module (line 117) and repeated go vet with piped/misredirected output that hid the exit code (lines 139, 151, 161). The orchestrator's continuation (line 167) wrongly stated that 10d09fde had 'partially fixed' storage/main.go. A third coder (1259c143) then did the repo-wide pointer refactor correctly, with build and vet green at lines 209/212. The second reviewer repeated the same X-Board search three times, tried nonexistent vendor/ paths, and was stopped by the loop_control judge (repeating_itself 0.84, line 267) before giving any verdict. The orchestrator's final message was a question to the user, and that message became the PR title and body. Reads always came before edits (0 violations). The navigation order was mostly respected; the exceptions were the ask agent calling list_symbols on a directory and the filesystem-wide find. Total: 98 turns, 128 tool calls, $1.98 and about 15 minutes of wall time for a roughly 45-line feature, more than half of it spent on scope outside the task.

strengths: The caching code follows the repo's existing GetLabels/getItems pattern exactly: same helpers, 24h TTL, X-cache header, board-prefixed keys.

The invalidation analysis is thoughtful: <board>:export is dropped on createLabel, comment writes invalidate board caches because comments are nested in item payloads, and createKanban invalidates the per-user board-id cache.
getKanban's plain-string response is handled with small helpers that match the file's style, instead of being forced through the JSON map path.
Reads always came before edits, and the final build and go vet both pass (trace lines 209, 212).
concerns: The PR title and body are an internal question to the user, not the PR description the task required.
The getItem cache key depends on an X-Board header this endpoint never required, which can leave item reads stale for 24h after writes.
The comment-write invalidation flushes the entire Redis keyspace when X-Board is absent.
A roughly 50-line unrelated RPC pointer refactor was bundled in to satisfy a harness vet gate.
No manual verification of the caching behaviour, and no completed reviewer pass before the PR was opened.
Budget: 98 turns and $1.98, more than half spent on a fix-up coder that made no edits, a scope-creeping refactor and a reviewer that looped.
overall_assessment.narrative: The core change is small, idiomatic for this repo and mostly correct, and the coder that wrote it worked efficiently. The run around it went badly. A pre-existing vet failure was treated as blocking and fixed with an unrelated repo-wide refactor. One fix-up agent burned its turn budget without editing anything, the orchestrator misdescribed that agent's work, the only real review was stopped for looping, and the required PR description was never written, so the PR went out titled with an internal status message. Fixing the title and body, making the getItem key independent of an optional header (or requiring that header), and ideally splitting out the RPC refactor would make this mergeable.
